summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No region-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for the department appears in the sources, so the operative facts for a visitor are the national ones.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but public-facility access is restricted by law. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. The exceptions cover custody, situations requiring medical attention, and accompaniment of an elder, a child under 12, or a person with disabilities; the bill also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', subject to the narrow listed exceptions. IDEHPUCP legal analysts Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte argue this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. They state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Ayacucho has no separate provision, enforcement action or incident on this point; the national ban applies to the region.

Violence against trans people is documented and rising. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty, including multiple gunshots and stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias in 2020.

The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. It contains no Ayacucho-specific finding; its value for this record is the national hate-violence data the regional assessment relies on.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard the April 2025 restroom law is argued to breach. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; per BBC News Mundo this was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional after an activist legal challenge.

Enforcement of the restroom restriction reaches private life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ayacucho live under the same national restroom statute as visitors, with no department-level variation in the sources. The bathroom ban's practical burden falls on local security staff, whose personal judgment and potential ID checks determine access, per activist Gianna Camacho's warning.

The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI data on 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020-2023 is national, with no Ayacucho-specific breakdown in the sources; the department's own incidence of anti-trans violence is therefore not separately quantified here.

Peru's June 2024 removal of pathologising terminology from official health guidance applies to healthcare settings in Ayacucho as elsewhere, a step described as advancing dignity for trans patients.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ayacucho-specific enforcement action, complaint, prosecution or incident involving the national restroom law appears in the sources; whether the article 5 restriction has been applied in the department is unresolved and not sourced.

The sources do not resolve whether Ayacucho's regional or municipal authorities have issued any implementing guidance, signage rules, or contrary protections under the national framework.

Whether the 2020-2023 homicide and violation figures include any cases in Ayacucho is not stated in the inventory and remains unresolved.
